name: Permissionless Blockchain
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Permissionless Blockchains: Trustless by Design
lesson.summary: A permissionless blockchain lets anyone join as a participant or validator without approval, substituting decentralized trust mechanisms for identity vetting.
lesson.body:
A permissionless blockchain is a network anyone can join, as a transacting user, a node operator, or a validator or miner, without asking anyone's permission first. There is no application process, no identity check, and no committee deciding who is allowed to participate. This sits at the opposite end of the spectrum from the permissioned model covered in the previous chapter, where a controlling entity explicitly authorizes each participant before they can act on the network.

The obvious question this raises is how a system can function, let alone be trusted with real value, if literally anyone, including people actively trying to cheat, is allowed to take part. The answer connects directly to decentralized trust: instead of vetting who is honest in advance, permissionless networks are engineered so that honest behavior is the economically rational choice even for total strangers who have never been screened at all. Proof of work makes cheating expensive by requiring real computational effort to propose a block, so an attacker attempting to rewrite history would need to outspend the combined effort of every honest miner. Proof of stake makes cheating expensive in a different way, by requiring validators to lock up their own capital as collateral that can be destroyed if they act dishonestly. In both cases, trust does not come from knowing who the other participants are; it comes from making dishonesty costlier than honesty, for anyone, regardless of identity.

Bitcoin and Ethereum are the two clearest examples. Anyone with a computer, appropriate software, and an internet connection can download the full software stack and begin operating as a node or, with the necessary hardware or stake, as a validator. No form is filed, no organization signs off, and the network has no mechanism to reject a new participant on the basis of who they are, only on the basis of whether they follow the protocol's rules.

This openness is genuinely valuable: it produces censorship resistance, since no single authority controls who can transact, and it removes any single point of control that a government, company, or hacker could pressure or seize to shut the network down. But it is not free. Reaching agreement among a large, open, mutually untrusted population takes longer and costs more than coordinating a small set of pre-approved validators, which is exactly why proof of work consumes significant real world energy and why proof of stake, despite being far more efficient, still requires meaningful capital to be locked up across the network. Coordinating protocol upgrades is also harder, since there is no central authority who can simply mandate a change; it requires broad voluntary agreement among participants who cannot be compelled to update.

It is worth being precise here, because permissionless is sometimes used loosely as a synonym for public, but they answer different questions. Permissionless is about who may participate and validate. Whether anyone can also read the resulting ledger is a separate question, taken up next.
